newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algiers shakes off fear to celebrate New Year.
newsitem.headline: Algiers shakes off fear to celebrate New Year.

text.p: Watched over by heavy deployments of police, Algerians ushered in the New Year with a burst of determined gaiety in their capital city.
"It's as if they were suddenly determined to ward off an evil fate," said one Algiers resident on Wednesday.

"Until Tuesday, it looked like New Year was going to pass unmarked. Shops were scarcely decorated at all and the usual seasonal chocolates had only made a timid appearance in the windows. There was no festive atmosphere at all because of all the killings...."
Bombs brought fear and carnage to Algiers in the dying days of 1996, four explosions killing 19 people and wounding 210.

Outside the capital, 82 people were slain in December in mass killings of civilians. Many had their throats cut and bled to death in the continuing violence, which the authorities blame on Moslem fundamentalists.

As the capital awoke and decided to celebrate, bakeries in the city centre were besieged. In the main shopping street, Rue Didouche Mourad, confectioner Montero worked behind closed doors, letting in small groups to be served.
At the ONCV (Office Nationale des Vins) wineshop it was a similar scene, with men of all ages queueing on the pavement.
Traffic jams snarled the city streets. Hotels put up "full" signs for their dinner-dances.

A line of cars stretched outside the Hotel El Djazair (former St. George) despite the 9,000 dinar ($164) cost of a ticket. At the Sofitel hotel, it was 26,000 dinars ($473) per couple. All were sold out.
Most big hotels included a room in the price of the ticket for the evening celebration, partly to help cut traffic accidents but mostly for their guests' safety.

Night is not a safe time to travel in Algeria, where at least 60,000 people have died in political violence since the authorities thwarted Islamists from a general election victory by scrapping the poll in 1992.
At midnight, ships outside Algiers Bay gave the first signal of the New Year, sounding their sirens and firing flares.
Gunfire crackled across the city once again -- this time celebrating the arrival of 1997 and fresh hopes of peace.
